claims.text: Pulumi components let you turn a group of resources into a reusable building block.
With Pulumi components, you can define a network, a database, or an application service once and share it across projects and teams.
People using a Pulumi component work with its inputs and outputs without needing to understand every resource inside it.
The legacy AWSX VPC component manages the VPC, subnets, route tables, and gateways behind a few lines of code.
Pulumi's new component state migrations let you ship the upgrade path with the component itself.
A Pulumi component state migration translates the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi works out which resources need to change.
With Pulumi component state migrations, component authors can change the internal design and include the migration in the same release.
The Pulumi state migrations API is experimental and may change.
Feedback on component state migrations can be shared in the discussion at https://github.com/pulumi/pulumi/discussions/24799.
The AWSX VPC example at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/tree/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration follows a network as requirements change over time, moving from v1 to v2 to v3.
The legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component creates a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and its association, and an internet gateway.
In the example, a security group sits outside the `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component and refers to the VPC.
Without a migration connecting old state to new code, an upgrade of the AWSX VPC component could replace the VPC instead of keeping it.
Replacing the VPC would require replacing the security group too, because the security group refers to the VPC's ID, per the AWS CloudFormation documentation on AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup VpcId.
The AWSX VPC example does not create a database.
The modern `awsx.ec2.Vpc` component preserves the existing network when upgrading from the legacy AWSX VPC component.
The third version of the example removes AWSX and declares the resources directly with `@pulumi/aws`.
In the third version of the example, Pulumi still manages the resources, but the user's code controls each resource instead of relying on the component to create it.
Across all three versions of the AWSX VPC example, the AWS resource IDs stay the same.
Across all three versions of the AWSX VPC example, the security group continues to use the same VPC.
In the AWSX VPC example's resource trees, `awsx:` entries are component records and `aws:` entries represent the AWS resources that stay in place.

In v1 of the example, the resource tree is rooted at `awsx:x:ec2:Vpc "vpc"` containing `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc "vpc"`, `awsx:x:ec2:Subnet "vpc-isolated-0"` (with its `aws:ec2/subnet:Subnet`, `aws:ec2/routeTable:RouteTable`, and `aws:ec2/routeTableAssociation:RouteTableAssociation` children named `vpc-isolated-0`), and `awsx:x:ec2:InternetGateway "vpc"` containing `aws:ec2/internetGateway:InternetGateway "vpc"`.

In v2 of the example, the resource tree is rooted at `awsx:ec2:Vpc "vpc"` containing `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc "vpc"`, which itself contains `aws:ec2/subnet:Subnet "vpc-isolated-1"` (with a nested `aws:ec2/routeTable:RouteTable "vpc-isolated-1"` and `aws:ec2/routeTableAssociation:RouteTableAssociation "vpc-isolated-1"`) and `aws:ec2/internetGateway:InternetGateway "vpc"`.

In v3 of the example, the resource tree is rooted at `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc "vpc"` directly containing `aws:ec2/subnet:Subnet "vpc-isolated-1"` (with a nested `aws:ec2/routeTable:RouteTable "vpc-isolated-1"` and `aws:ec2/routeTableAssociation:RouteTableAssociation "vpc-isolated-1"`) and `aws:ec2/internetGateway:InternetGateway "vpc"`.
Pulumi's state records both the physical resources and the components that group them.
Each record in Pulumi's state has a Pulumi name, called a URN.
Managed resources in Pulumi's state also have an ID from the cloud provider, such as an AWS VPC ID.
The legacy AWSX component wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate components.
Modern AWSX removes the wrapper components around the subnet and internet gateway and puts the managed resources under different parents.
In the example, the Pulumi name of the subnet changes from `vpc-isolated-0` to `vpc-isolated-1` when moving from legacy to modern AWSX.
Pulumi aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible.
Upgrading from legacy to modern AWSX needs to remove component wrappers and transfer references to the resources that take their place.
A Pulumi state migration describes the whole change of removing component wrappers and transferring references together.
To move an existing network to modern AWSX, you register the new VPC component with an alias for the legacy component type and a migration callback through the `stateMigrations` option.
The `migrateClassicVpc` function comes from the example's migration file at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/blob/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts.
A Pulumi component's alias lets Pulumi find the old component.
The migration callback receives the old component's saved state, followed by the state of its children.

The migration callback copies the saved state records, changes their names and parents to match modern AWSX, and returns `newState` (the complete set of records that should replace the old component and its children) and `successors` (a map from each old URN that disappears to the URN that takes its place).
The full migration code for the first migration is available at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/blob/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts.
The first checks in the migration callback make it safe to run again: if the state already uses modern AWSX or plain AWS resources, there is nothing to do.
In the migration callback, an unexpected component type raises an error instead of guessing how to migrate it.
The `rename` helper in the example's migration code copies the saved record and changes its URN, type, and parent.
The `rename` helper preserves the AWS resource ID and the other saved fields.
In the example, the `rename` helper moves the subnet under the managed VPC.
The two subnet entries in `successors` let the Pulumi engine know that the old component wrapper and the managed subnet point to the same new subnet record.
Pulumi uses the `successors` mappings to update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack.
In the example, the security group lives outside the VPC component, but its reference to the VPC still needs to be valid after the migration.
The VPC successor mapping keeps the security group's reference connected to the migrated VPC record, which retains the same AWS VPC ID.
The third version of the example declares the VPC, subnet, route table, association, and internet gateway directly with `@pulumi/aws`.
The second migration changes who defines the resources in the user's program, and the user can then adjust their configuration in a separate update.

The second migration, available at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/blob/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v3/migration.ts, removes the AWSX VPC component record and moves the managed VPC into its place.
In the second migration, both the old component and its VPC child map to the new VPC record.
In the second migration, the VPC keeps its AWS ID, and the other resources remain beneath it.
The VPC registration in the example keeps aliases for both previous component types and both migration callbacks.
Pulumi runs the migration callbacks in order, passing each result to the next callback.
A stack still using legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to the plain AWS version in this example.
A stack already using modern AWSX skips the first migration in this example.
Once both migrations have run in this example, both callbacks return no result on later updates.
Keeping earlier migrations with the component means its users can skip versions without having to edit stack state by hand.
After a migration changes saved state, Pulumi compares the new program with that state and calls the provider for any remaining changes.
Keeping resource IDs does not mean every upgrade has an empty preview: the example can still show in-place updates for provider defaults and tags.
To try the example, you start with `v1` and follow its README.
To try the example, you should use the same stack, backend, project name, AWS region, and availability zone for each version.

Before each upgrade in the example, running `pulumi preview` should show the existing VPC, subnet, route table, association, internet gateway, and security group with no creates, deletes, or replacements.
Pulumi preview evaluates the migration without saving it, and the update saves the migrated state.
If you maintain a Pulumi component, you can register the migration inside its implementation and ship both together.
With a shipped component migration, users do not need to write the migration, attach the callback, or edit their stack state.
When users upgrade the component and run Pulumi, Pulumi runs the migration as part of the normal preview and update.
For an internal change that keeps the same component inputs and outputs, users can keep their existing component calls.
The component state migrations guide at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ covers the callback contract.
The VPC example at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/tree/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration contains all three programs and the migration code shown in the post.
State migration callbacks run during Pulumi previews and updates when prior state exists.
State migration callbacks must be idempotent.
State migration callbacks return no result when the state no longer needs migration.
State migration callbacks rewrite state without performing provider operations.
A component state migration is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.
A component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings for any changed URNs.
In a component state migration's successor mappings, each mapping connects an old URN omitted from the result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
If no migration is needed, the component state migration callback returns no result.
The option reference at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/statemigrations/#callback-api explains the state migration callback API.

The state entries for component state migrations use the checkpoint resource format documented at https://pulumi-developer-docs.readthedocs.io/latest/docs/references/deployment-schema.html#pulumi-resource-state.
The checkpoint resource format includes fields such as `urn`, `type`, `id`, `parent`, `provider`, `inputs`, and `outputs`.
A state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using update plans.
A state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using targeted updates.
The restrictions on state-changing migration results do not require removing an already-applied state migration.
